meta.audience: The people of Nephi, assembled at the temple, with their wives and children present
meta.location: The temple in the land of Nephi

world_behind.title: A temple sermon, commanded the night before
world_behind.text: Verse 11 has the word coming to Jacob with a time and a place: get up into the temple on the morrow. The temple was built in 2 Nephi 5, and this is the first sermon the record places inside it. Jeremiah's temple sermon works the same way — a prophet stationed in the sanctuary to tell the assembly that their standing there proves nothing.

world_behind.title: The two royal prohibitions, in order
world_behind.text: Deuteronomy 17:17 forbids a king to multiply wives and to multiply silver and gold. The previous chapter reported the people doing both, in that order, under their second king. This chapter takes them in the same order and treats them as one problem with two faces.

world_behind.title: Whoredom, used literally
world_behind.text: In the Bible the word is overwhelmingly a figure for idolatry — twenty-three occurrences in Ezekiel and twelve in Hosea, nearly all of them about worshiping other gods. Jacob uses it for what men are doing to their wives. The transfer is deliberate and it is the reason the Lord's speech in verses 31 through 33 sounds like a covenant lawsuit.

world_behind.title: Scripture cited as a permit
world_behind.text: Verse 23 states the mechanism: the people "understand not the scriptures, for they seek to excuse themselves." The precedent they are using is David and Solomon, who are in the brass plates. This is the record's first case of a community reading its own canon for license, and the answer given is not that they misquoted but that they misread.

world_behind.title: Wives and children in the room
world_behind.text: Verse 7 names them as present and as the reason the sermon is hard to give. Prophetic rebuke in the Bible is normally addressed to a body politic; here the injured parties are standing in the audience while the injury is described, and the preacher says so.

world_behind.title: A branch from Joseph, not from David
world_behind.text: Verse 25 announces a righteous branch from the loins of Joseph. Jeremiah 23:5 raises the righteous Branch to David. The substitution is quiet and it is the theological ground for the whole colony's existence, offered here as the reason the marriage law is stricter than the ancestors' practice.

world_behind.title: A law with a reservation attached
world_behind.text: Verse 30 leaves the Lord free to command otherwise for the raising of seed. Ancient law codes seldom publish their own exception; this one does, in the same breath as the commandment, which is why the passage has been read in two directions ever since.

words.text: Not gravity of mood but steadiness of mind — the King James sense is sound judgment, the opposite of being carried away. Jacob magnifies the office with soberness, which frames the whole sermon as deliberate rather than heated, and the ten verses of hesitation that follow are the word being demonstrated.

In the King James Bible the delicate are the sheltered, and Deuteronomy's covenant curse falls hardest on "the tender and delicate woman." Jacob applies it not to bodies but to minds and feelings, twice, and both times to the people who have done nothing wrong. The word marks the sermon's real cost.

Here in its plain old sense — on family terms, close, unguarded. The instruction is to think of your brethren as yourselves and be familiar with all, which asks for a dismantling of social distance rather than an act of charity. The distance, not the money, is what verse 13 said was wrong.

Used twice and nowhere else. It is comparative, and the comparison is to the pride he has just spent ten verses on. Jacob is not saying pride is minor; he is saying there is something worse coming, and having graded the two he never revisits the ranking.

phrases.term: that I might rid my garments of your sins
phrases.text: The previous chapter said blood; this one says sins. Benjamin will say blood again. The garment figure stays constant across all three and only the stain changes, which suggests the image was fixed tradition and the substance was the speaker's own to specify.

phrases.term: the word which healeth the wounded soul
phrases.text: His audience came for this and he cannot give it. The phrase occurs once in scripture and it appears in a sermon that goes on to say the opposite is required today. Naming the sermon they should have received is how Jacob measures what he is about to do.

phrases.term: have daggers placed to pierce their souls
phrases.text: The image is of a weapon set, not thrown. Jacob is describing the effect of his own words on innocent hearers, and he assigns himself the agency. Few preachers in this record admit that the necessary sermon will injure the people who least deserve it.

phrases.term: under the glance of the piercing eye of the Almighty God
phrases.text: The eye appears twice in this chapter and nowhere else, and its second appearance is a threat rather than a witness. Here the eye watches the preacher deliver; five verses later it can smite the hearers to the dust. The same faculty is comfort and danger depending on where you are standing.

phrases.term: the hand of providence hath smiled upon you most pleasingly
phrases.text: "Providence" occurs once in this record and only twice in all of scripture; it names God's arrangement of circumstance rather than his speech or his law, and Jacob deploys it exactly where the people would have said "we prospered." The compliment is real and it is the setup. He grants the wealth its divine source before he touches the pride, which is why the argument never becomes an argument against wealth. The turn comes at "because some of you have obtained more abundantly."

phrases.term: wear stiff necks and high heads because of the costliness of your apparel
phrases.text: Nephi used this exact pair of images for the churches of the last days. Jacob uses it for the congregation in front of him, roughly sixty years after the family left Jerusalem. The costliness of apparel is introduced here and becomes the record's standing marker for a society coming apart.

phrases.term: But before ye seek for riches, seek ye for the kingdom of God
phrases.text: The order is the whole instruction. It does not forbid the second term, and verse 19 explicitly permits it with conditions attached — hope in Christ first, and then a stated intent, itemized in four verbs. Wealth is put under a sequence rather than under a ban.

phrases.term: the one being is as precious in his sight as the other
phrases.text: The flattest statement of human equality in the record, and its grounding is unusual. Not shared dignity but shared origin and shared purpose: all flesh is of the dust, and all of it was created for the same end. Equality is argued from creation and telos rather than from rights.

phrases.term: they understand not the scriptures, for they seek to excuse themselves
phrases.text: Cause and effect run backward from what one expects. The failure to understand is produced by the wish to be excused, not the other way around. The chapter's diagnosis of misreading is moral before it is intellectual.

phrases.term: David and Solomon truly had many wives and concubines
phrases.text: The concession is granted in full before it is refused. The Lord does not dispute the history; he disputes the inference. It is the shortest verse in the passage and it does all the work, because once the precedent is admitted and condemned the appeal has nowhere left to go.

phrases.term: I, the Lord God, delight in the chastity of women
phrases.text: The clause has no parallel in scripture. Delight is an affection, not a statute, and placing it here makes the marriage law an expression of what God enjoys rather than of what he prohibits. The prohibition follows in the next clause and reads as the consequence.

phrases.term: the sobbings of their hearts ascend up to God against you
phrases.text: Ascending cries are the language of Abel's blood and of Israel in Egypt — the sound that reaches God and starts a judgment. Applied to wives in a congregation, it makes private grief a legal instrument, and it is the last thing Jacob says before the chapter ends.

verses.label: v. 1–4
verses.title: Credentials and dread
verses.text: The heading dates the sermon to after Nephi's death, and Jacob then spends three verses on his own standing: the responsibility he is under, the office he is magnifying, the diligence they can vouch for, and the anxiety that is new today. Every claim is about him, not them, and it buys him the right to what comes next.

verses.label: v. 5–11
verses.title: The apology before the accusation
verses.text: He can tell them their thoughts; the sin is abominable; it grieves him; it shames him; he must use boldness before their wives and children; those wives came for healing and will get daggers. Then two verses of warrant: a strict command, and a word that arrived with a time and a place attached. Seven verses of reluctance in front of a rebuke that has not started, ending with the audience being told the sermon was assigned.

verses.label: v. 12–16
verses.title: Pride, diagnosed
verses.text: Riches obtained, unequal distribution, hearts lifted, necks stiff, heads high, apparel costly, brethren persecuted. The chain is causal and it moves from an economic fact to a social behavior in one verse. The two exclamations that follow are not argument; they are a man wishing his hearers could see what he sees.

verses.label: v. 17–21
verses.title: The correction, with money left in
verses.text: Be familiar, share substance, seek the kingdom first, then seek riches for named purposes, and remember that the person you despise came from the same dust for the same end. This is the only place in the passage where Jacob tells them what to do rather than what they are, and it is notably unascetic.

verses.label: v. 22–26
verses.title: The turn, and the misused text
verses.text: Pride is closed off, a grosser crime announced, and the floor given to the Lord. The accusation is a charge of misreading — they seek to excuse themselves out of what was written — and the answer runs through Joseph rather than through David, which resets whose precedent governs this people.

verses.label: v. 27–33
verses.title: The law and the reason for it
verses.text: One wife, no concubines, because God delights in chastity; and then the reason, which is not a statute but a sound. He has heard the sorrow and the mourning of the daughters of his people, in Jerusalem and here. The law is issued and then justified by the crying it is meant to stop.

verses.label: v. 34–35
verses.title: Worse than the Lamanites
verses.text: The closing comparison is the one calculated to land hardest on this audience, and the damage listed is domestic: broken hearts, lost confidence of children, bad examples, sobbing. The chapter that began with a man dreading to wound ends by counting wounds he did not cause.

chapter.title: The sermon narrates its own difficulty
chapter.text: Ten of thirty-five verses are about how hard this is to say. No other discourse in the record spends a third of itself on the preacher's reluctance. The effect is that the rebuke arrives as something suffered rather than enjoyed, and Jacob is careful to establish that before a single accusation is made.

chapter.title: Two sins, one root, unequal treatment
chapter.text: Pride gets eleven verses and a remedy; the marriage offense gets thirteen and a commandment, delivered in God's own voice. Jacob grades them explicitly. The grading matters because the second offense is the one where the injured party is present in the room.

chapter.title: Riches are not the problem and the chapter says so twice
chapter.text: Providence gave the wealth, and verse 19 permits seeking it. What is condemned is comparison — "because some of you have obtained more abundantly than that of your brethren" — and the behaviors comparison produces. The economics of the chapter are about distance between people, not about quantity.

chapter.title: Scripture is shown failing in the hands of readers who want something
chapter.text: The people have the record of David and Solomon and have drawn a permission from it. The Lord's reply concedes every fact and denies the inference. It is a durable warning about canonical precedent, and it is delivered inside the canon itself.

chapter.title: The law is grounded in hearing rather than in order
chapter.text: Verses 31 through 33 do not argue from creation, from covenant structure, or from social consequence. They argue that God has heard weeping. The women in this chapter never speak, and their sound is the thing that produces the commandment.

chapter.title: The exception in verse 30 is placed where it cannot be missed
chapter.text: Immediately after the commandment, the Lord reserves the right to command otherwise. Publishing the reservation alongside the rule makes the rule conditional in a way that a later reader cannot claim to have discovered, and the chapter does not soften either half.

chapter.title: The comparison at the end reverses the colony's self-image
chapter.text: The people whose whole identity is being not-Lamanites are told they have done greater iniquities than the Lamanites. Jacob will develop this in the next chapter. Here it lands cold, in the last two verses, after the audience has already been told they are breaking their wives' hearts.

applications.title: Say the hard thing on purpose
applications.text: Jacob prepared, named his reluctance, and did it anyway. If there is something you owe someone and have not said, the chapter's method is: get clear on your standing, admit the cost out loud, and then say it plainly.

applications.title: Audit for comparison, not for amount
applications.text: The chapter's test is not how much you have but what having more has done to how you see people. Pick one relationship where a gap exists, and ask honestly which direction you are looking.

applications.title: Be familiar
applications.text: The instruction is social before it is financial. Choose one person you keep at a polite distance and close it — talk to them the way you talk to family.

applications.title: Put the sequence back in order
applications.text: Write down what you are currently seeking and in what order. Then write the order verses 18 and 19 give, including the four purposes, and see where yours diverges.

applications.title: Check what you are excusing yourself from
applications.text: The people were reading real scripture badly because they wanted an outcome. Name one teaching you have found a reason to set aside, and ask whether you reasoned your way there or arrived first.

applications.title: Listen for the sobbing
applications.text: The chapter treats unheard grief as evidence. Ask the people closest to you what your example has cost them, and be prepared to hear an answer.

questions.text: Am I more anxious about the welfare of anyone's soul than I was a year ago, and what changed?
Whose wounds have I enlarged while trying to say something true?
What do I own or wear or do that is functioning as a claim to be better than someone?
If someone charted what I actually seek first, what would the chart show?
Do I treat any category of person as less precious in God's sight, and would I admit it if I did?
Whose confidence have I lost, and do I know why?
